In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no evidence to suggest that the pH of the storage fluid is the major determinant in the changes in potassium and DPG content of stored blood, although the changes are accentuated by the acid pH of CPD and are reduced by correcting the blood gas and the pH of stored blood to physiological range.
, in general, the blood gas and electrolyte changes that occur during storage are reversible and that the changes in DPG and potassium content of stored red cells are closely interrelated.
, although blood gas correction of stored blood does reduce the plasma potassium content, it does not restore it to normal levels, and the red cell DPG does not increase to normal levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the blood gas and acid-base status of stored blood has a profound effect on the DPG and plasma K+ content of red cells, but that these parameters do not return to their normal levels except when the blood is stored less than 7 days.

the blood gas and acid base status of CPD blood should be corrected to physiological levels prior to transfusion, especially if the blood is to be used for the transfusion of patients with myocardial ischaemia.
